newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary BUX hits 3rd closing high in a row.
newsitem.headline: Hungary BUX hits 3rd closing high in a row.

text.p: Hungarian shares powered to a new closing record on Friday propelled by gains of high-caps MOL Rt and OTP Bank.
The BUX index of the Budapest Stock Exchange closed on Friday at a preliminary 7,149.03 points, up 154.73 points or 2.21 percent.
Analysts said the Budapest Stock Exchange's short-term outlook remained positive despite recent strong gains but on the longer term growth could slow down.

"I have a feeling that some of the corporate earnings growth is going to slow down in the second half of the year," said Andrew Thomson, head of European emerging markets research at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London.
"Some of the earnings of chemicals like TVK or Borsodchem could even go down in the second half of their year as plastics prices are going to go down".
However, he said fundamentals in Hungary remained good and the Budapest market was likely to remain attractive. "Hungary in fundamentals is still looking good," Thomson said.
Traders said that Thursday afternoon chemicals Borsodchem, OTP and MOL rose significantly in London (on the SEAQ) and this rise left its impact on the Budapest bourse.
"It was obvious that the rally would continue (in Budapest) and everybody wanted to buy," said Attila Berecz of Raiffeisen Securities.
Friday's main gainers were OTP which advanced to 5,650 forints, up 435, pharmaceuticals Egis Rt that put on 650 forints to end at 13,300, and oil and gas company MOL which rose to 4,330, up 140.

James Oates, director for central and eastern Europe at UBS in London, said earlier today that Hungary's safe heaven position in the region was behind Friday's rise, meanwhile the amount of funds reaching the Budapest market was not that much.
"People still regard Hungary a safe heaven and I think probably this may be the case until after the Polish elections," Oates said. Polish parliamentary elections are scheduled for September 21.
Thomson, however, said Hungary was likely to remain attractive compared to Poland even after the elections.
"The corporate sector in Hungary is doing so much better than the Polish," he said.
